extracted.intended_audience: general readers, genre writers, and researchers interested in science fiction & fantasy magazines
extracted.subtask_description: A descriptive profile of Lightspeed magazine covering its format, publication practice, editorial history, special-issue/crowdfunding activity, and awards — useful for writers researching markets or readers researching the magazine's stature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue content composition
rubrics_metrics.description: "The magazine published four original stories and four reprints in every issue, in addition to interviews with the authors and other nonfiction."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All content in each issue is available for purchase as an ebook and for free on the magazine's website. This defines the magazine's regular content mix (originals + reprints + nonfiction/interviews).

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication frequency / schedule
rubrics_metrics.description: "Frequency: Monthly" — the first issue was published in June 2010 and it has maintained a regular monthly schedule since.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates a steady, recurring publication cycle authors can expect and that the magazine produces frequent opportunities for publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format and distribution channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Lightspeed is described as an "American online fantasy and science fiction magazine" whose content is "available for purchase as an ebook and for free on the magazine's website."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary distribution is online; back issues/collections are sold as ebooks while web content is freely accessible. This affects readership, discoverability, and compensation/rights expectations for contributors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audio/podcast availability
rubrics_metrics.description: "Lightspeed also made selected stories available as a free podcast, produced by Audie Award–winning editor Stefan Rudnicki."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selected stories are adapted to audio, expanding audience and providing additional exposure for authors; signals the magazine invests in multimedia presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional-market status (SFWA-qualifying)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Lightspeed became an SFWA-qualifying market in July 2011."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being SFWA-qualifying signals professional-level pay/standards and can matter for authors seeking SFWA membership or counting the market toward professional credentials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special issues and crowdfunding practice
rubrics_metrics.description: In September 2013 Lightspeed announced a Special Issue titled "Women Destroy Science Fiction," an anthology entirely written and edited by women; "This issue was funded via Kickstarter, earning $53,136 with an original goal of $5,000."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows the magazine runs themed special issues and leverages crowdfunding to expand projects; successful crowdfunding enabled further volumes ("Women Destroy Fantasy" and "Women Destroy Horror"). Useful for authors/agents evaluating opportunities for themed submissions or anthology participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awards, nominations, and reprint recognition (prestige metrics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lightspeed was a finalist for the Hugo Award for Best Semiprozine in 2011–2013 and won in 2014 and 2015; its podcast won a Parsec award; multiple stories were finalists/nominated for Nebula and Theodore Sturgeon awards; several stories were reprinted in prominent Year's Best anthologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The extensive award history and frequent reprints indicate the magazine's reputation for high-quality, award-caliber fiction and is a measure authors use to assess magazine prestige.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial leadership and ownership history
rubrics_metrics.description: "Lightspeed is ... edited and published by John Joseph Adams." Founded/run by Sean Wallace (Prime Books) with Adams as editor; Adams purchased Lightspeed and Fantasy Magazine in November 2011 and combined Fantasy Magazine's content/staff into Lightspeed in January 2012.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial leadership and ownership changes (and the absorption of Fantasy Magazine) describe the magazine's editorial direction, staffing, and potential shifts in submission focus or policy over time.
